current_criteria.name: logical_consistency
current_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether the answer contains any internal contradictions — i.e., conflicting claims about the same entity, state, or action — within its own text. It applies ONLY to semantic or temporal inconsistencies that arise from the answer’s own wording, such as: 'The person is both sitting and standing', 'The object is both visible and invisible', or 'The door is open and closed'. It does NOT evaluate: (1) factual accuracy against the visual image (handled by visual_grounding), (2) external real-world plausibility (handled by biological_or_realistic_plausibility), (3) interpretive ambiguity or stylistic vagueness (handled by specificity or visual_grounding), or (4) hallucinations or unsupported claims — unless they create internal contradictions. If an answer contains no internal contradictions, it is considered logically consistent and should not be penalized, even if it is factually wrong or visually ungrounded. When comparing two answers that are both logically consistent, preference should be determined by other criteria (e.g., visual_grounding, factual consistency, or completeness). This criterion is inapplicable if the answer contains no claims, is empty, or is entirely hallucinated without self-contradiction — in which case, the worker should evaluate other criteria or flag ambiguity. Workers must strictly avoid conflating logical consistency with visual accuracy or factual truth — internal coherence alone is sufficient to satisfy this criterion.

current_criteria.name: action_or_state_accuracy
current_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether the answer correctly infers or describes a dynamic state or action (e.g., walking, opening, jumping, leaning) based on visual cues — motion blur, posture, trajectory, or implied temporal change — and applies ONLY when the question explicitly or implicitly requires such inference (e.g., ‘What is the person doing?’, ‘Is the door open?’, ‘What is the fire hydrant doing?’, or ‘Is the cat running?’). It does NOT apply to static object identification, spatial layout, compositional descriptions (e.g., ‘in a line’, ‘balanced frame’), or questions about object type or structure unless they explicitly involve motion or state change (e.g., ‘leaning into a turn’ is valid; ‘wearing a hat’ is not). For questions asking about static states (e.g., ‘standing’, ‘wearing a hat’), the criterion is inapplicable — preference must be determined by visual grounding, factual consistency, or hallucination avoidance. Visual evidence must be clear and unambiguous for a definitive claim — if ambiguous, the answer must use calibrated uncertainty (e.g., ‘possibly walking’, ‘not clearly open’) and must NOT make speculative claims. Hallucinated or unsupported state/action claims (e.g., ‘the cat is dancing’, ‘the door is closing because of wind’) are penalized — even if the question does not explicitly ask about motion, any claim not visually supported is a hallucination. Accuracy is measured solely on whether the inferred state/action matches visual evidence — not on detail level, aesthetic quality, or contextual plausibility. When the criterion is inapplicable, workers must defer to other criteria (e.g., visual grounding, factual consistency) to determine preference — the criterion’s inapplicability is not a judgment but a scope constraint. When the criterion is applicable and both answers are equally accurate, defer to visual grounding or factual consistency. Workers must explicitly check for motion cues before applying this criterion — if no motion is visible, any claim of motion is a hallucination. The criterion does NOT evaluate whether an action is physically plausible or semantically reasonable — only whether it is visually supported. Any inference must be grounded in visual evidence — even plausible inferences (e.g., ‘waiting to pick up’) are invalid if contradicted by visual cues. If the question asks about static states, compositional layout, or object identification, this criterion is inapplicable — preference is determined by visual grounding and hallucination avoidance. This criterion does not override factual accuracy or visual grounding — if an answer is factually wrong or visually ungrounded, it is penalized under those criteria regardless of action/state inference. Workers must not use this criterion’s inapplicability to justify choosing a wrong answer — if the criterion is not triggered, preference must be determined by other criteria. This criterion is only for evaluating motion/state inference — not for evaluating object presence, absence, or static attributes.

current_criteria.name: avoidance_of_hallucination
current_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether the answer introduces any visual elements (objects, attributes, actions, spatial relationships, or identities) that are definitively absent from the image — not misidentifications, not plausible inferences, not contextually reasonable interpretations, and not stylistic or metaphorical language — and penalizes only such fabricated claims. A hallucination is defined as a claim that contradicts visual evidence and introduces content not present in the image, regardless of its plausibility, perceived severity, or contextual relevance. Misidentifications (e.g., calling a red box a Coca-Cola box) or factual errors (e.g., mislabeling color or object type) are not hallucinations — they are evaluated under visual grounding or factual consistency. Interpretive, metaphorical, or aesthetic language (e.g., ‘harmony’, ‘festive’, ‘abstract composition’) is exempt if visually grounded — e.g., ‘the scene evokes harmony’ is acceptable if the layout supports balanced composition — but not if it fabricates a non-existent object (e.g., ‘a golden dragon appears’). Hallucinations are penalized only when they are unqualified and definitively unsupported — qualified claims (e.g., ‘possibly a red umbrella’) are acceptable even if visually absent. Visual evidence must be cross-checked for every claim: if an element is visible, even if mislabeled, it is not a hallucination. If an element is not visible, it must be explicitly flagged as uncertain (‘not clearly visible’, ‘possibly’) to avoid penalization. The criterion is inapplicable when the answer is purely interpretive, metaphorical, or stylistic — as long as it does not fabricate visual content — or when the visual evidence is ambiguous and the answer uses calibrated uncertainty. Hallucinations are binary: present or absent — no partial credit or severity weighting. The criterion should not be used to penalize reasonable inferences (e.g., ‘the person is walking’ based on posture) if they are visually supported — only unsupported or fabricated claims are penalized. Workers must prioritize visual fidelity over textual caution, and defer to visual grounding or factual consistency if the answer is factually correct even if less specific or more cautious. This criterion is not about factual accuracy or contextual plausibility — only about visual presence or absence. Accuracy is measured solely by whether the claim is visually supported or not — not by how ‘obvious’ or ‘plausible’ the hallucination appears.

current_criteria.name: biological_or_realistic_plausibility
current_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates only whether an answer’s description of a living being (human or animal) is anatomically accurate or behaviorally consistent with known biological facts — e.g., a dog sniffing the ground is plausible; a dog flying is not. It applies ONLY when the visual evidence clearly identifies a living being and the answer describes its anatomy, posture, motion, or species-typical behavior. It does NOT apply to: (1) inanimate objects (e.g., keyboard, car, logo), (2) clothing, attire, or spatial context unless they imply biological behavior (e.g., a person leaning forward to pick something up), (3) emotional states, personality traits, or social roles (e.g., ‘arrogant’, ‘serious’, ‘politician’), (4) quantitative or spatial claims (e.g., ‘to the left’, ‘two meters away’), or (5) background elements. If the subject is not a living being, or if the visual evidence is ambiguous or insufficient to identify one, this criterion is inapplicable and must be ignored. When applicable, the answer must not hallucinate anatomical impossibilities or species-specific behavioral violations (e.g., a cat riding a bicycle, a human with extra limbs). Biological plausibility is assessed ONLY after visual grounding and factual consistency are confirmed — if an answer is visually ungrounded or factually incorrect, this criterion is inapplicable and should not be used to override other criteria. Hallucinated details — even if biologically plausible — are penalized because they violate visual grounding. When visual evidence is unambiguous and supports a biologically plausible description, the answer is preferred — but only if it also satisfies visual grounding and factual consistency. If two answers are equally visually grounded and factually correct, and one is more biologically plausible, the more plausible one is preferred — but only if it does not introduce hallucinations or contradict visual evidence. This criterion is strictly secondary — it never overrides visual grounding or factual consistency, and must never be used as a tiebreaker or default preference rule. Workers must explicitly note inapplicability when the subject is not a living being or when visual evidence is insufficient. Examples of inapplicability: ‘a red chair’, ‘a logo’, ‘a person wearing a hat’ (unless the hat implies biological behavior like ‘wearing a hat to keep warm’). Examples of applicable use: ‘a cat arching its back in fear’, ‘a dog sniffing the ground’, ‘a human holding a tool’. Workers must not confuse biological plausibility with visual fidelity — if visual evidence contradicts a biologically plausible claim, the visually accurate answer is preferred. Always defer to visual grounding and factual consistency first. This criterion is not for evaluating aesthetic, interpretive, or metaphorical language — only for anatomical or behavioral accuracy of living beings.

current_criteria.name: calibrated_uncertainty
current_criteria.description: Calibrated uncertainty applies ONLY when an answer is both factually correct and visually ambiguous — meaning the visual evidence is genuinely insufficient to support a definitive claim (e.g., object partially obscured, identity unclear, count uncertain due to occlusion). The answer must use qualifiers like ‘possibly’, ‘likely’, ‘not clearly visible’, or ‘appears to be’ to reflect this visual ambiguity — but only if the visual evidence supports it and the answer is not masking a factual error. This criterion is inapplicable if: (1) the answer is factually incorrect or hallucinated (e.g., claiming a cat is a dog), (2) the visual evidence is clear and unambiguous (e.g., a visible Apple logo), or (3) the answer is confidently correct even if not fully specific (e.g., ‘three chairs’ is acceptable if clearly visible). Calibrated uncertainty must never be used to justify or mask factual errors — such errors are penalized under visual grounding or factual consistency. Workers must first verify factual correctness and visual grounding before applying this criterion — if either is violated, the criterion is inapplicable and the answer is disqualified under other criteria. Uncertainty qualifiers must reflect actual visual ambiguity — not speculative reasoning, contextual assumptions, or stylistic vagueness. A confidently correct answer is always preferred over a hedged one if visual evidence supports certainty. This criterion is solely for signaling visual uncertainty — not for evaluating factual accuracy, completeness, or stylistic quality — and must not be used as a tiebreaker or default preference tool. Examples of appropriate use: ‘possibly a dog’ (ambiguous posture/shape), ‘not clearly visible’ (obscured text). Examples of inappropriate use: ‘a cat, possibly greyish-white’ (color clearly not greyish-white — factual error), ‘the door is open’ (clearly closed — no ambiguity).

current_criteria.name: completeness
current_criteria.description: Completeness evaluates whether an answer includes all visually verifiable and semantically relevant elements necessary to fully answer the question — without hallucinating, fabricating, or adding unsupported details. It is strictly secondary to visual grounding and factual consistency: any answer that is factually incorrect or hallucinated under multimodal_alignment or avoidance_of_hallucination is automatically disqualified from completeness evaluation. Completeness is only applied after visual grounding and factual accuracy are confirmed. An answer is preferred if it covers all visible, question-relevant components (e.g., object identity, position, action, or interaction), even if minor or nuanced (e.g., posture, direction, or background context). It does not reward verbosity, speculative inference, or aesthetic language unless it is visually grounded and semantically relevant. Omitting a clearly visible, question-relevant element (e.g., a person’s action in a question about movement) is a failure of completeness, but omitting non-essential or ambiguous elements (e.g., background texture) is not penalized. Workers must prioritize accuracy over coverage and flag cases of visual ambiguity by using calibrated uncertainty rather than fabricating details. Completeness rewards contextually reasonable inferences (e.g., inferring ‘clean and professional’ from white attire) as long as they are visually supported — but penalizes hallucinations (e.g., adding a nonexistent object or misrepresenting motion) even if they seem plausible or ‘more complete’. Examples: ‘a woman sitting at a desk’ is complete; ‘a woman sitting at a desk, wearing a hat’ is complete if the hat is visible; ‘a woman sitting at a desk, wearing a hat and holding a sword’ is incomplete if the sword is hallucinated. Always defer to visual evidence: if an element is not visible, its omission is not a failure of completeness — its addition is a hallucination. Completeness does not penalize interpretive or aesthetic language grounded in visual cues — e.g., ‘layered composition’ or ‘balanced framing’ — as long as they are contextually plausible and visually supported. Finally, completeness is not about quantity or exhaustiveness — it’s about faithful, relevant coverage of what is visible, and is strictly secondary to visual grounding and factual consistency. It is inapplicable when the question is meta, abstract, or does not require visual description. Workers must not use completeness to justify or mask factual errors — such errors are penalized under other criteria first.

current_criteria.name: multimodal_alignment
current_criteria.description: Multimodal alignment evaluates whether every textual claim in the answer is strictly grounded in visually verifiable elements from the image — meaning claims must be directly supported by observable evidence, and any hallucinated, fabricated, or unsupported details (including misidentifications or fabricated absence) are penalized. This criterion applies only to questions requiring literal, factual, or object-level visual descriptions — not aesthetic, stylistic, interpretive, or abstract responses. It does not evaluate semantic accuracy, factual correctness, or contextual plausibility — only visual fidelity. An answer is aligned if it contains no hallucinations, and is penalized if it fabricates or misrepresents visually present elements (e.g., claiming a visible object is missing, or inventing an object not in the image). It does not penalize reasonable, contextually grounded inferences (e.g., ‘the person appears to be walking’ based on posture) if they are visually supported and not speculative. Visual ambiguity must be handled with calibrated uncertainty (e.g., ‘possibly’, ‘unclear’) — not by fabricating details. Hallucinations — including both presence and absence — are strictly prohibited and must be penalized regardless of plausibility. When comparing two answers, if one contains hallucinations and the other does not, the hallucinated answer is always inferior. If both are hallucinated, the answer with fewer hallucinations (or more visually grounded elements) is preferred — but only if the hallucinations are objectively comparable in scope. If neither answer is fully aligned, the one with the least severe hallucination is selected. The criterion does not apply to abstract, hypothetical, non-visual, or meta-information questions — in which case, workers should defer to other criteria. Examples: ‘a red umbrella’ is hallucinated if no umbrella is visible; ‘the person is holding a pen’ is acceptable if a pen is visible; ‘the scene feels cozy’ is acceptable if it’s an aesthetic description and not hallucinated. Workers must verify each claim against the image with literal visual evidence — not context or inference — and must not use this criterion to penalize omission of non-visual or ambiguous details. This criterion is secondary to visual grounding and factual consistency — if an answer is factually incorrect, it may be penalized under those criteria regardless of alignment. Accuracy is measured by strict visual fidelity — any hallucinated claim disqualifies an answer — even if it is factually correct or plausible. Workers must prioritize literal visual grounding over interpretive or contextual inferences — and must reject any answer that contains even one hallucinated claim, unless explicitly qualified with uncertainty (which is not allowed for hallucinations).

current_criteria.name: temporal_coherence
current_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether the answer’s description of motion, dynamic action, or implied temporal sequence (e.g., ‘jumping’, ‘falling’, ‘opening’, ‘running’) is visually consistent with clear indicators of motion or implied time progression — such as blurred motion, directional posture, trajectory lines, or dynamic body orientation. It applies ONLY when such visual motion cues are present and unambiguous; if motion is absent, ambiguous, or inferred from static posture (e.g., ‘sitting’, ‘standing’, ‘leaning’), the criterion is INAPPLICABLE and must be explicitly flagged — workers must NOT use it to resolve preference between candidates or as a tiebreaker. When applicable, the answer must not contradict the visual evidence (e.g., claiming ‘landing’ when the person is clearly airborne). Speculative or cautious inferences (e.g., ‘possibly jumping’) are acceptable IF grounded in visual motion cues, but not if they contradict them. The criterion is NOT about factual plausibility (e.g., whether ‘browsing’ is physically possible) or structural object accuracy (e.g., ‘ramp’, ‘bowl’) — those are evaluated under visual grounding or factual consistency. Temporal_coherence does not override or justify preference over other criteria — if inapplicable, workers must defer to visual grounding, multimodal_alignment, or avoidance_of_hallucination to break ties. If both answers are temporally consistent, the criterion is inapplicable and preference is determined by other criteria. Hallucinated motion or unsupported temporal claims are penalized under avoidance_of_hallucination, not under this criterion — this criterion only evaluates consistency with visual motion cues. Workers must first verify visual grounding and factual consistency before applying temporal_coherence — if either is violated, the answer is disqualified regardless of temporal consistency. The criterion does not evaluate static spatial relationships (e.g., ‘on the left side’) or compositional dynamics — those are handled by visual grounding or specificity. Inapplicability does not imply preference — it simply means this criterion cannot be used to evaluate or resolve the comparison. Workers must explicitly note ‘inapplicable’ when no motion cues are present or ambiguous, and must not infer motion from static posture or compositional context. Examples: ‘The person is airborne mid-jump’ is consistent with blurred motion — valid; ‘The person is jumping’ when the person is clearly standing — inconsistent — invalid; ‘possibly falling’ when posture suggests descent — acceptable if motion cues support it; ‘sitting on a chair’ — inapplicable, defer to visual grounding.

current_criteria.name: visual_coherence
current_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether the answer’s spatial, compositional, or contextual relationships between visually described elements are consistent with the spatial layout and relative positioning of objects in the image. It applies only when the answer describes multiple objects, their relative positions (e.g., ‘left of’, ‘behind’, ‘in front of’), or spatial configurations (e.g., ‘centered’, ‘symmetrical’, ‘overlapping’). It does not apply to single-object descriptions or questions that do not involve spatial reasoning. An answer is penalized if it misrepresents spatial relationships (e.g., claiming ‘the cat is behind the dog’ when the dog is clearly behind the cat), or if it invents spatial interactions not supported by the image. It also penalizes inconsistent framing or perspective (e.g., describing an object as ‘on the left’ when it’s clearly centered from the viewer’s perspective). The criterion is inapplicable when the answer is ambiguous about spatial relationships or when the visual evidence is too occluded to verify position — in such cases, calibrated uncertainty should be used instead. Evaluation is done by cross-checking every spatial claim against the image’s layout, with preference given to the answer that aligns with visual evidence. Unlike visual grounding, this criterion focuses specifically on relational and compositional accuracy — not individual object identity or presence. It is distinct from logical_consistency because it evaluates spatial truth, not internal contradictions. Workers must prioritize visual evidence over semantic assumptions — for example, ‘the person is standing beside the table’ is valid if visually confirmed, even if the table is partially obscured. This criterion should not be applied to abstract or non-spatial questions, and should never override visual grounding or factual consistency. The goal is to ensure spatial descriptions are not only accurate but also contextually coherent within the image’s visual frame.

all_criteria.name: visual_grounding
all_criteria.description: The answer must accurately reflect what is visible in the image — describing elements, positions, colors, textures, or actions that can be directly observed. An answer is preferred if it avoids speculation or assumes unseen elements.

all_criteria.name: question_relevance
all_criteria.description: The answer must directly address the question without drifting into irrelevant topics. It should match the question’s intent — e.g., if the question asks about arrangement, the answer should focus on spatial or compositional details, not background stories or unrelated facts.

all_criteria.name: factual_consistency
all_criteria.description: The answer must be factually consistent with the visual evidence. If the image shows a cat, it should not be described as a dog. If an object is partially visible, it should not be claimed to be fully present or absent.

all_criteria.name: avoidance_of_hallucination

Hallucinations are penalized even if they appear plausible or are common in real life. Evaluation is done by cross-checking every claim in the answer against the visual evidence. For example, claiming ‘a red umbrella is being held by the person’ when no umbrella is visible is a hallucination. This criterion applies to all answers, regardless of question type, and is inapplicable when the answer is purely interpretive or metaphorical (e.g., ‘the scene feels hopeful’) — but only if such interpretations are visually grounded. Accuracy is measured by whether hallucinated content is absent or explicitly flagged as uncertain.

Examples: ‘a woman sitting at a desk’ is complete; ‘a woman sitting at a desk, wearing a hat’ is complete if the hat is visible; ‘a woman sitting at a desk, wearing a hat and holding a sword’ is incomplete if the sword is hallucinated. Completeness does not penalize interpretive or aesthetic language grounded in visual cues — e.g., ‘layered composition’ or ‘balanced framing’ — as long as they are contextually plausible and visually supported. Finally, completeness is not about quantity or exhaustiveness — it’s about faithful, relevant coverage of what is visible, and is strictly secondary to visual grounding and factual consistency.

all_criteria.name: specificity
all_criteria.description: The answer should provide precise, detailed, and concrete descriptions — e.g., specifying ‘left eye’ rather than ‘eye’, or ‘blood near mouth’ rather than ‘blood on face’. Vague or general statements are less preferred.

all_criteria.name: calibrated_uncertainty
all_criteria.description: When the visual evidence is ambiguous or incomplete, the answer should acknowledge uncertainty — e.g., ‘possibly’, ‘likely’, or ‘not clearly visible’ — rather than asserting certainty. Overconfidence in unsupported claims reduces quality.

all_criteria.name: clear_language
all_criteria.description: The answer should be grammatically correct, easy to understand, and free of unnecessary jargon or ambiguity. Clarity enhances accessibility and ensures the human evaluator can quickly assess the quality without confusion.

all_criteria.name: coherence_and_structure
all_criteria.description: The answer should be logically organized — with clear transitions, consistent terminology, and a logical flow — so the viewer can follow the description without mental effort. Disorganized or contradictory phrasing reduces credibility.

all_criteria.name: biological_or_realistic_plausibility
all_criteria.description: For questions involving animals or humans, the answer should align with known behaviors or anatomy — e.g., a zebra should not be described as “curious” if the context suggests it’s a prey animal. Plausibility enhances trust and realism.

It does NOT evaluate: (1) factual accuracy against the visual image (handled by visual_grounding), (2) external real-world plausibility (handled by biological_or_realistic_plausibility), (3) interpretive ambiguity or stylistic vagueness (handled by specificity or visual_grounding), or (4) hallucinations or unsupported claims — unless they create internal contradictions. Workers must strictly avoid conflating logical consistency with visual accuracy or factual truth — internal coherence alone is sufficient to satisfy this criterion.

all_criteria.name: multimodal_alignment
all_criteria.description: The answer must align with the visual modality — for example, describing objects that are clearly visible, not relying on auditory or textual context that isn’t supported by the image. Evaluated by cross-checking visual evidence with textual claims.

all_criteria.name: action_or_state_accuracy
all_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether the answer correctly identifies or infers a dynamic state or action (e.g., walking, running, opening, closing, jumping) based on visual cues — motion blur, posture, object position, or implied temporal change — and must be inapplicable if the question does not involve such inference. It does not apply to static object identification, spatial layout, text reading, or compositional descriptions unless they are directly tied to motion or state change (e.g., 'leaning into a turn' is valid; 'in a line' is not). For static states (e.g., 'standing', 'wearing a hat'), the criterion does not apply — such descriptions are evaluated under visual grounding or specificity. Workers must first determine if the question is action/state-oriented before applying this criterion. all_criteria.name: contextual_sensitivity
all_criteria.description: The answer should respect the contextual setting of the image — e.g., recognizing indoor vs. outdoor, formal vs. casual, or cultural cues — and tailor its response accordingly. Evaluated by assessing whether the answer ignores or misinterprets contextual clues.

all_criteria.name: temporal_coherence
all_criteria.description: For sequences or implied motion, the answer must be consistent with the temporal progression shown — e.g., if the image captures a person mid-jump, the answer should not describe them as having landed. Evaluated by analyzing motion cues or implied time states.

manager_prompt:
List and describe 10 criteria for how human annotators compare the quality of two answers to the same visual question.

The task is RLHF-V style preference comparison for visual question answering and image-text responses. The worker model will receive:
- the image,
- the source question,
- candidate answer A,
- candidate answer B.

Focus on human preference factors such as visual grounding, question relevance, factual consistency with the image, avoidance of hallucinated visual details, completeness, specificity, calibrated uncertainty, and clear language.
